title: Dense Feature Tracking of Atmospheric Winds with Deep Optical Flow

problem.claim: Atmospheric winds are important across natural hazards, energy transport, ocean currents, large-scale circulation, and ecosystem fluxes, but observing them is complex.

gap.claim: NASA's Earth Observation System has a large gap in atmospheric-wind observations, and large-scale satellite-based observations are lacking.

contributions.claim: WindFlow is a machine-learning-based system for feature tracking of atmospheric motion using optical flow.
The approach uses high-resolution GEOS-5 Nature Run simulations for supervised learning and transfers the learned model to satellite images.
Among four compared network and learning architectures, RAFT produces the lowest errors across wind-speed and wind-direction metrics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The deep-learning optical-flow approach scales to ultra-high-resolution images of size 2881x5760 with less than 1 m/s bias and 2.5 m/s average error.
Held-out numerical outputs show RAFT performs well across spatial, temporal, and physical dimensions.
Comparison with an operational AMV product against rawinsonde observations indicates that RAFT transfers across simulations and thermal-infrared satellite observations.

narrative_sequence.summary: Atmospheric winds are consequential, while observing them is complex and underrepresented in NASA's Earth Observation System.
AMVs estimate cloud movement from sequences of multispectral satellite images, and optical-flow methods can produce dense vector fields.
WindFlow applies machine-learning-based optical flow, trained on GEOS-5 Nature Run simulations and transferred to satellite imagery.
The authors report resolution, bias, and error results; compare four architectures; and assess held-out outputs and transfer to satellite observations.
The work presents machine-learning-based optical flow as an efficient approach for robust, large-region AMV feature tracking.

source_observation.claim: High-resolution numerical simulations were used for supervised learning and transfer to satellite images because large-scale satellite-based observations were unavailable.

interpretation.claim: When labeled observations are scarce, simulation-trained models may provide a pathway to learning and cross-domain transfer.

application.claim: Use high-resolution domain simulations as a training source for remote-sensing models, then evaluate transfer to observational imagery.

exception.claim: Transfer performance may depend on the similarity between simulations and target observations; the abstract does not specify the limits of transfer.

source_observation.claim: RAFT had the lowest reported errors among four compared architectures across wind-speed and wind-direction metrics.

interpretation.claim: Architecture comparison can identify a model that better preserves both magnitude and directional accuracy for dense motion estimation.

application.claim: Compare multiple optical-flow architectures using task-specific speed and direction metrics before selecting a deployment model.

exception.claim: The abstract does not provide the compared architectures, metric values, or evaluation conditions beyond the stated summary.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the four compared architectures.
The abstract does not report dataset sizes, training details, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not establish independent verification beyond the reported comparisons.
